capture.final_message:
Split the outer conjunction into two independent standard facts.

- For the ideal statement, apply the Krull/Zorn maximality argument: consider ideals containing \(I\) whose underlying sets remain disjoint from \(S\). Chains have unions with the same properties, so choose a maximal such ideal \(p\). To show \(p\) is prime, if \(xy\in p\) but \(x,y\notin p\), maximality forces both enlarged ideals \(p+(x)\) and \(p+(y)\) to meet \(S\). Multiplying the two resulting witnesses gives an element of \(p\cap S\), a contradiction.

- For the equivalence, observe that both sides hold unconditionally. The left side is the usual primality criterion: if \(n>1\) were composite, a proper nonzero divisor \(m<n\) would satisfy \(\gcd(n,m)=m\ne1\). The right side says that the canonical embedding
  \[
  \operatorname{Multiset}(\text{irreducible associates})\to \operatorname{WithTop}(\cdot)
  \]
  preserves addition, so \(\operatorname{some}(a+b)=\operatorname{some}(a)+\operatorname{some}(b)\).

Thus each direction of the `Iff` can establish its target directly, without using the opposite hypothesis.
